blocks.text: Retrosynthesis is the opposite of synthesis. It breaks the target molecule down, on paper, into less complicated, simpler and more readily available compounds that can serve as starting materials, using the disconnection approach. The bonds disconnected are those that give a considerable structural simplification; after a series of disconnections we arrive at simple, easily available starting materials.

blocks.caption: Terms used in retrosynthesis
rows: an open-ended arrow meaning 'can be made from'
the imaginary breaking of a bond in the TM to move towards simpler starting materials
a fragment, often an ion, produced by a disconnection; a building block for the synthesis
a real reagent that does the job of a synthon, which is usually too unstable to use itself
converting one functional group into another to reach the target
a diagram of all possible disconnections and synthons from the TM back to starting materials

blocks.alt: Top: target molecule and starting materials joined by two open retrosynthetic arrows (break the TM down on paper) and a single arrow back (build the TM up in the laboratory). Bottom: aniline (TM), FGI to nitrobenzene with a red slash on the C-N bond, disconnection into a phenyl anion (synthon A, SE benzene) and NO2+ (synthon B, SE nitric acid).
blocks.caption: Synthesis, retrosynthesis and the terms used (original diagram after Figures 25.1 and 25.2).
blocks.long_description: Retrosynthesis is planned backwards from the target; the synthesis is then carried out forwards. For aniline, the amino group is first changed on paper into a nitro group (FGI), because a nitro group can be put on benzene directly. Disconnecting the C-N bond then gives two synthons, a phenyl anion and the nitronium ion, whose real reagents are benzene and nitric acid.
